title: Smallpox in Delhi
hook: he nurses the sick during an epidemic in Delhi and dies of it at eight, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Guru at five, and Chhajju the water-carrier who explained the Gita. Your line was small, and wise. Who was the quiet teacher in your day? Day seventy-three.

Most of us remember what a city feels like when a sickness is loose in it. The empty streets. The fear of touching a door handle. Families keeping their distance from their own grandparents. And the people who went in anyway: nurses, cleaners, delivery drivers, neighbors carrying soup. In 1664, while the child Guru Har Krishan was staying in Delhi, an epidemic swept the city. Tradition names it smallpox, and some accounts add cholera. People were dying in the lanes. The eighth Guru was about seven years old, and a guest in a stranger's house. He could have left. Today, what a child did in a frightened city.
screen: `A CITY WITH A SICKNESS LOOSE.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO WENT IN ANYWAY.` → `DELHI, 1664.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the young Guru did not hide. He went among the sick of Delhi, Hindu and Muslim alike, comforting them and tending to them, and his followers with him. The house where he was staying, Raja Jai Singh's bungalow, had a well, and tradition says the Guru blessed its water and gave it to the sick. People came in crowds. Then the child caught the disease himself. Sikhs tell of his last days with great tenderness. He was burning with fever, and he stayed calm. His followers, frightened, asked who would lead them after him. Tradition says the dying boy gave a short, puzzling answer: Baba Bakale. The Baba, the next Guru, is at Bakala, a village in Punjab. He said no more. That riddle is tomorrow's story and the day after's. He died in Delhi in 1664, not yet eight years old. And here is what a visitor to Delhi can still see. The bungalow became Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, one of the best-known gurdwaras in the city. Beside it lies a large pool, fed, tradition says, from that same well, and people still take its water home to the sick. The langar there feeds huge numbers of people every day. During the COVID-19 pandemic, gurdwaras in Delhi, Bangla Sahib among them, cooked and delivered meals to people who couldn't leave home. A child's service in one epidemic, echoing in another, more than three hundred and fifty years later.
screen: `AMONG THE SICK OF DELHI.` · `WATER FROM THE WELL.` · `BABA BAKALE.` · `GURDWARA BANGLA SAHIB TODAY.` · then, large: `HE SERVED THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check on someone unwell. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is sick right now, in body or in spirit. A friend in the hospital. A parent with a long illness. Someone having a hard month. Hold them in your mind without trying to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, just wish them ease, breath by breath. And decide how you'll reach them today. The bell holds the time.
Smallpox in Delhi. In 1664 the child Guru Har Krishan tended the sick in an epidemic, caught it, and died, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands.
Your line: he served the sick. Today, reach out to the person you thought of: a call, a text, a meal left at the door. Day seventy-three.

what a scholar hears: the accounts name smallpox, some with cholera; the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh became Gurdwara Bangla Sahib.
